messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Viktor's Story

Viktor was fifty-six when the accident happened, a professional dancer who had spent thirty-five years perfecting his craft. He had danced in regional ballet companies across the Northeast, taught at studios, choreographed for smaller productions—work that had given his life shape and meaning. His marriage to Elena had weathered the irregular hours and modest income because they shared a life built around movement, artistry, and the particular discipline that dance demanded. He was not a star, but he was respected, known in his circles as someone who could still command a studio, who understood bodies and music with an almost intuitive grace.

The accident occurred at a charity gala in late September. Viktor was performing a contemporary piece he had choreographed, a solo that required him to move rapidly across the stage while maintaining visual connection with the audience. The lighting had been adjusted that afternoon; he had rehearsed the piece a dozen times in the weeks prior, but never under the exact configuration of lights and sound that the venue's technical team had set up. During the third performance of the evening, as he executed a series of turns near the stage edge, his spatial awareness—usually his greatest asset—failed him. He misjudged the distance to the edge and collided with a young stagehand named Marcus who had moved into his path to adjust a light fixture. The impact was violent enough that Marcus fell backward, striking his head against a metal support beam. Viktor watched him lose consciousness before the music stopped.

Marcus survived, but suffered a traumatic brain injury that left him with significant cognitive and physical deficits. He was thirty-two years old. He would not return to stagehand work. The guilt that Viktor carried after that moment was not the abstract guilt of someone who had made a mistake; it was the specific, crushing knowledge that his body—the instrument he had spent a lifetime learning to control—had destroyed another person's future. He had come to believe, with absolute certainty, that he should have been more cautious, that a truly protective person would have been aware of every person in the space, that his failure to do so was unforgivable. The thought that he might never atone for what he had done became the lens through which he saw himself.

That conviction shaped everything that followed. Within weeks, Viktor began avoiding the studio where the accident had occurred, then the neighborhood where it stood. He stopped accepting teaching positions that required him to work in crowded spaces where bodies moved unpredictably around him. When he encountered certain songs—particularly the piece he had been performing that night, but also any music with a similar tempo or emotional register—his mind would flood with images of Marcus falling, and he would spiral into recriminations about what he should have done differently. Each trigger seemed to confirm his deepest fear: that he was fundamentally incapable of being the protector he was supposed to be, that he had failed in the role that mattered most. The weight of that conviction drove him to suppress any thought about the accident itself, to push away memories and conversations, to try not to think about Marcus or the injury or the moment itself. But the suppression never held. His mind would circle back, and each time it did, he would feel the guilt deepen, feel the proof of his failure accumulating.

Elena noticed the changes first. Viktor had always been someone who could move through crowded spaces with ease, who thrived in the collaborative chaos of rehearsals. Now he would tense when they went to restaurants or shops. His sleep had fractured; he would lie awake beside her, his body rigid, unable to relax even in the darkness of their bedroom. He had come to believe that staying alert—that hypervigilance—was the only way he might prevent another catastrophe, that relaxing was itself a form of negligence. His concentration at work deteriorated. When he did take on teaching engagements, he found himself unable to focus on the dancers in front of him; instead, his attention fragmented, scattered across invisible threats. He dwelt increasingly on how he used to be before September—the confident, capable artist who moved through the world with certainty. That person felt gone, replaced by someone he no longer recognized.

By the time Viktor came to his first appointment, it had been eight months since the accident. He described himself as trapped in a loop he could not break. He was afraid that his guilt was justified, that he truly was the failed protector he feared he had become. What he wanted, more than anything, was to understand whether he could ever be whole again—or whether the person he had been was permanently lost.
